did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm portrays disbelief as an attitude of the heart: the fool says, “There is no God,” and as a result, his actions are described as corrupt and detestable.
Did you know? The LORD is described as looking down from heaven and examining humanity to see whether there is anyone with understanding—anyone who seeks God.

Did you know? This verse makes a sweeping indictment: everyone has turned away and become corrupt; there is not even one person who does good. The repetition of the word “none” emphasizes the severity of the moral condition.

Did you know? The expression “those who devour my people eat bread” portrays evildoers as people who harm the nation routinely, as though eating bread were an everyday act; it is also said of them that they do not call on the LORD.

Did you know? Although the wicked are described as those who do not call on the LORD, the verse declares that they will be overwhelmed with fear, because God is present among the generation of the righteous.
Did you know? The verse contrasts “the poor man’s counsel” with the LORD: the wicked shame or frustrate the poor man’s plans, but he can trust that the LORD is his refuge.
Did you know? The psalm concludes with a prayer for Israel’s salvation from Zion and for the LORD to restore His people, ending in joy: Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.
Did you know? Using the names “Jacob” and “Israel” in the same verse creates a parallel between the two names of the people and emphasizes that the salvation and restoration concern all Israel.
